Patient Vignette: "Amir"

Amir is a 56-year-old married man of Middle Eastern descent who presents as articulate and meticulously dressed, though his posture is rigid and his eyes rarely meet mine for more than a moment. He works as a social media manager for a mid-sized nonprofit, a job he describes as "managing chaos" - scheduling posts, monitoring comments, and crafting messaging around social justice issues. He has been married for twenty-eight years and has two adult children.

The traumatic event occurred approximately fourteen months ago. Amir was driving home from a late community meeting in a gentrifying neighborhood. He was stopped at a red light when a police cruiser pulled up behind him, lights flashing. Within seconds, two officers were at his window, ordering him out of the car. He had not committed any traffic violation. The officers claimed he matched the description of a suspect in a nearby robbery. Amir, who speaks with a slight accent despite decades in the country, tried to explain calmly that he was a resident, a professional, a father. He remembers the larger officer grabbing his arm, twisting it behind his back, and slamming his face against the hood of his car. He was handcuffed, searched, and held on the curb for forty-five minutes while they ran his license. When they finally released him, there was no apology. He drove home with a split lip and a bruise blooming across his cheekbone.

In the weeks that followed, Amir stopped driving at night. Then he stopped driving altogether, taking the bus or asking his wife to drive him. His work required him to be online constantly, but he began to dread opening his phone. Every notification, every flashing blue light on his screen, triggered a jolt of adrenaline. He started posting less frequently, then stopped responding to comments. His supervisor noticed he was "disappearing" from the team chat. Amir told her he was fine, just tired.

At home, his wife describes him as "a ghost." He sits in his armchair after dinner, scrolling through news feeds about police violence, reading the same articles until his eyes burn. He cannot sleep. When he does, he dreams of the cold metal of the handcuffs, the grit of the pavement against his cheek. He wakes up clawing at his own arms, trying to get the handcuffs off. Some nights he wakes his wife by shouting, "I didn't do anything!"

He avoids the neighborhood where it happened entirely, taking a forty-minute detour on the bus. He flinches when a car backfires. He has not attended a single community meeting since the incident, despite being a longtime organizer. His social media feed, once a vibrant mix of event promotions and solidarity posts, is now a graveyard of unread messages and half-finished drafts. He tells me he feels "hollowed out," like someone scooped out the part of him that believed in fairness, in safety, in being seen as a good man. He says he watches his colleagues post about police reform with a kind of numb cynicism. "They don't know," he whispers. "They have no idea what it feels like to be a suspect in your own country."

When I ask him what he wants from our sessions, he shrugs. "I just want to sleep," he says. "And I want to stop feeling like I'm still on that curb."
